cards.explanation: The answer is True. David says it right at the start: "I will sing and make music with all my being." All his being, friends. That's not a little hum while you're doing dishes. That's the whole man in it, and I'd be out of breath by the second line. (Psalm 108:1)

The answer is among the nations. David says, "I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing Your praises among the peoples." He doesn't say it just once, either. Nations, then peoples, so the song goes out wide. This man is not saving his singing for a small room. (Psalm 108:3)

The answer is beyond the heavens. David says, "For Your loving devotion extends beyond the heavens…" Then he adds that God's faithfulness "…reaches to the clouds." That's a lot of reach, friends. My own reach stops where the top shelf starts. (Psalm 108:4)
The answer is False. David prays, "Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your glory cover all the earth." That's every corner of it, not only Israel. Not even a crumb gets left out. (Psalm 108:5)

The answer is that David asks God to save them with His right hand. He prays, "Respond and save us with Your right hand, that Your beloved may be delivered." He's asking for rescue, plain and simple. I think a prayer that short and clear is a good one to borrow. (Psalm 108:6)
The answer is False. The psalm says God has spoken from His sanctuary: "I will triumph!" There's no warning in those first words, friends. It opens with a win. (Psalm 108:7)
The answer is True. God says, "Gilead is Mine, and Manasseh is Mine…" He claims both, the region and the tribe. Nobody has to wonder whose they are. Not a single sticky note needed. (Psalm 108:8)

The answer is triumph. God says, "over Philistia I shout in triumph." It echoes how God opened, with "I will triumph!" The same word shows up at the start and again here in verse 9. Triumph, friends, from the top. (Psalm 108:7, 9)

The answer is the fortified city. David asks, "Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom?" Two questions, back to back, and both are about being led. I think he's asking who's got the map. (Psalm 108:10)

The answer is True. David asks, "Will You no longer march out, O God, with our armies?" It comes right after, "Have You not rejected us, O God?" Those are two hard questions in a row. I think this is a man being honest with God, and he doesn't stop there. (Psalm 108:11)

The answer is that the help of man is worthless. David's reason is this: "Give us aid against the enemy, for the help of man is worthless." He asks God for aid, and he says why in the same breath. I think that's a man who knows where to look. David says it plainly, and so does the psalm. (Psalm 108:12)

The answer is that God will trample them. The last line says, "With God we will perform with valor, and He will trample our enemies." Notice who does the trampling, friends. It's God, and David's people get to be valiant alongside Him. That's a strong way to end a song that had some hard questions in the middle. (Psalm 108:13)
